families.name: Bantu
families.description: Largest language family in Kenya (~65% of population). Spread across central, western, and coastal regions.

families.name: Nilotic
families.description: Second largest family (~30%). Includes Plains Nilotes (Maasai, Turkana, Samburu, Teso), Highland Nilotes (Kalenjin, Pokot), and River-Lake Nilotes (Luo).

families.name: Cushitic
families.description: Found in northern and eastern Kenya (~3%). Includes Somali, Borana/Oromo, Rendille, and Daasanach (Dhaasanac).

families.name: Other
families.description: Includes Swahili (Bantu-based national & official lingua franca), English (official), and minor language isolates.

languages.name: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
languages.notes: Largest mother-tongue community in the central highlands (Kiambu/Kabeti, Murang'a/Metumi/Fort Hall, and Nyeri/Gaki around Mount Kenya [Kĩrĩnyaga / Kĩreĩra / Donyo Egere]); documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. V–VI, pp. 220–221, 234–236, 286–309 [361], 362–366, 371–375 — audited 100% line-by-line across the Aug. 23, 1887 Ngongo Bagas blood-brotherhood with Miani, Karanja & Waiyaki, all 68 parallel ravines from Nairobi to Thegu incl. the Chania liana suspension bridge, 600-ft. Maragua gorge & 700-ft. Mathioya chasm, Subugo forest fortifications, kihingo gates & ngurunga pitfalls with muriju [Acokanthera Schimperi] poison, 'U-u-u-ui! Ngai!' & 'Mirema!', Muthamaki/Athuri & Anake, mburi ya thayu & kuhoria tatha chanting 'Thayu! Thayu!', Aturi smiths, ruhiu, kahiu, kiondo, mwatũ, njohi/uhi, njingiri, corno & 7–8 ft. muro digging-sticks, 3-tier ridge crop zoning, chiefs Kihara, Gathirimu, Getura, Karanja wa Maragua, Wamugunda of Tetu, Sept. 16 Mathira 7-step githathi peace covenant over a white ram & black goat, Chief Kihura at Ndoro, and the Oct. 8–14, 1887 first ascent of Mount Kenia across 5 vertical zones to 15,355 ft. [4,680 m] with Lobelia Telekii Schweinfurth), Hémery (1903), Hinde (1904), McGregor (1904), W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa'), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', pp. 559–576, Ex. 2–3, 8, 10, 14).

languages.name: Dholuo (Luo)
languages.notes: River-Lake Nilotes of the Lake Victoria basin; documented in Rev. Charles New (1873), Rev. Thomas Wakefield & Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. XI.D 'Nile Sub-Group', pp. 273–287: XXI. Kavirondo on Victoria Nyanza pp. 284–285, Wakefield's MS Kavirondo Vocabulary from a Swahíli caravan traveller, and first comparative proof of marked affinity with I. Shilluk/Dyur [Luoh/Lwo, Bellanda & Dembo] pp. 275–276, XVIII. Lúr [Luoh] pp. 282–283 & XX. Shúli [Gani/Shefalu] pp. 283–284), Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902), Northcote (1907), Roscoe/Willis (1915), Mill-Hill Fathers (1920), BFBS (1921), and Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', pp. 559–576, Ex. 2–3, 10, 13, 15–16: academic title prefixes & Sheng sibilant substitution 'shrubbing' sida, shitikashel, aishishi).

languages.name: Kalenjin
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Nandi, Kipsigis/Lumbwa [Il Kakesan], Tugen/Kamasia [Kapteberewa & Nderois], Marakwet & Endo/Ndo [Chebleng], Keiyo/Elgeyo, Cherang'any, Kabkamat/Olmo, Sangwirr, Uasin Gishu Moiven/Muttia/Il-Mokwan/I-Sirikwa, Sabaot, Pökoot); documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894, Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 383–384: Kamasia hills [5,500–7,000 ft.] and Kerio valley grain trade with the Elgeyo and Marakwet yielding 65 loads of mtama and wimbi in Nov.–Dec. 1887), Hobley (1902, 1903, 1910), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis (1909 'The Nandi: Their Language and Folk-Lore'), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), BFBS (1921), Rottland (1982), Creider & Creider (1983, 1989), Toweett (1979), Mietzner (2016), Jerono (2018), Sitienei Jepkoech (2018), Diercks & Rao (2019), Landman (2019), Kouneli (2021), and Joost Zwarts, Andrew Chelimo & Prisca Jerono (2023; 2024 'The reflexive in Kalenjin: Its syntactic status and semantic functions', Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 539–556, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11210482).

languages.name: Luhya (Luyia)
languages.notes: 17+ Western Bantu dialects including Wanga (Luhanga of Buhanga), Bukusu/Masaba (Lubukusu), Kabras, Nyala, Marama, Tsotso, Tiriki, Idakho (Lwitaxo), Isukha, and Maragoli (Logoori / Luragooli [rag] JE41); documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902, 1919), Purvis (1907, 1909), Roscoe (1915), Rev. N. Stam (1929 'The Bahanga', Catholic Anthropological Conference Vol. I, No. 4, pp. 143–179 — audited 100% line-by-line), and Doris L. Payne, Sara Pacchiarotti & Mokaya Bosire, eds. (2016 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.281 — audited 100% line-by-line across Ch. 9 Eleanor Glewwe & Ann M. Aly 'Coronal palatalization in Logoori' pp. 165–183 [sj → ʃ, /h/-plosivization h → b / N__, nasal deletion], Ch. 11 Hannah Sarvasy 'The future in Logoori oral texts' pp. 201–219 [6 future inflections SP-ra- -a, na-SP- -e, SP-raka- -e / SP-aaka- -e, SP-rika- -e, SP-ri- -a, naa-SP- -e & 4 future constructions], Ch. 12 Meredith Landman 'Quantification in Logoori' pp. 219–234 [vuri vs. 15-class -oosi], Ch. 15 John Gluckman & Margit Bowler 'The anticausative alternation in Luragooli' pp. 271–289 [-Vk telic anticausative & Class Ia/Ib transitive roots], Ch. 25 Ken Safir & Naga Selvanathan 'Niger-Congo transitive reciprocal constructions and polysemy with reflexives' pp. 495–512 [Lubukusu -an + ba-b-eene khu b-eene], and Ch. 28 Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka 'Humor in Kenyan comedy' pp. 559–576 [Ex. 9 & 11 on ilisemanga, kuipia & enclitics -ko/-nga]).

languages.name: Kamba (Kĩkamba)
languages.notes: Central Bantu language of Eastern Kenya across 4 regional divisions (Ulu/Yulu [kīkamba kīluŋgalu & Kīluŋgu], East Ukamba/Kitui [aþaisu / kīþaisu], Kīkumbuliu & Mumonī, plus Anoka on Mt. Noka and the 1836 Rabai diaspora); documented in Krapf (1850), Last (1885), Hinde (1904), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Gerhard Lindblom (1920 'The Akamba in British East Africa: An Ethnological Monograph', 2nd Ed., Enlarged, Archives d'Études Orientales Vol. 17, Uppsala, pp. I–XII, 1–607, Figs. 1–167 — audited 100% line-by-line), BFBS (1921), Michieka & Muaka (2016, Ch. 28, p. 569, Ex. 12), and Jones & Freyer (2019).

languages.name: Somali
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language of North Eastern Kenya; documented in Krapf & Isenberg (1840, pp. iv–v, xi, xiii), Rigby (1850, 1866), Burton (1856), Hunter (1880), Robert Needham Cust (1883, Vol. I, Ch. IX.C.I 'Somáli', pp. 119, 121), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, pp. 10–12, 33, 123–124, 162, 174: 8-man Somali bodyguard led by 24-year-old Habr-Anwal headman Qualla Idris with Juma Jussuf, Ali Hassan, Mahommed & Kharscho, and Somali botanical term likke for Hydnora africana), de Larajasse (1897), Kirk (1903, 1905), BFBS (1921), Morgan Nilsson (2016 'Somali gender polarity revisited', in Doris L. Payne, Sara Pacchiarotti & Mokaya Bosire, eds., 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 23, pp. 451–466, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.494 — audited 100% line-by-line across Tables 1–15 & Ex. 1–11 on penultimate vs. final tonal accent, Corbett's agreement criterion, stem-syllable plural definite article selection, 5th-declension collectives dibí-d-a vs. regular plurals dibi-yá-d-a, Arabic broken plurals, lexical collectives, corporate nouns & generic singulars), Kimper et al. (2019), and Nurse (2019).

languages.name: Kisii (Ekegusii)
languages.notes: Eastern Lake Victoria Bantu language of the Kisii Highlands; documented in Hobley (1902) and Johnston (1902, 1919).

languages.name: Meru (Kĩmĩĩrũ)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya & Tana valley Bantu cluster (Imenti, Tigania, Igembe, Mwimbi, Chuka, and Kĩtharaka); documented in Hobley (1910), Champion (1912), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Kithaka wa Mberia (2004), and Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', p. 562, Ex. 1: Majimoto's Meru wordplay on Swahili wizi wa mabavu 'violent robbery' vs. Meru mbavu 'ribs' & prenasalized Mbro).

languages.name: Maasai (Maa)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Eastern Nilotic, across 4 Clans ['L-Aiser, Il-Meñgana, Il-Mokesen, Il-Molelyan], 2 Moieties ['L-oodo-kishu & 'L-oorook-kishu], 19 Sub-Families [Il-gilat], and 5 Districts [Il-Kaputiei, En-aiposha, 'L-Oitai, Il-Kisonko, 'L-Uasinkishu], plus Laikipiak, Segellai, and Tigirri); documented in Krapf (1854 'Vocabulary of the Engútuk Eloikób'), Erhardt & Krapf (1857 'Vocabulary of the Enguduk Iloigob'), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Robert Needham Cust (1883, Vol. I, Ch. X.A.V–VI, pp. 149–152), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. I–IV & VI, pp. 12–14, 84, 100, 131, 206–236 [285], 367–385 — audited 100% line-by-line), Hildegarde Hinde (1901), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis & Sir Charles Eliot (1905), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), W. S. & K. Routledge (1910), BFBS (1921), Tucker & Mpaayei (1955), and Jonathan Moodie (2016 'Number marking in Lopit, an Eastern Nilotic language', in 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 397–416, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.492: Eastern Nilotic tripartite number marking and Maasai Greater Plural eng-ker 'sheep' → ing-kerr-a 'sheep [pl.]' → ing-kerr-ai 'herds of sheep' in Table 18, p. 412).

languages.name: Turkana (Ng'aturukana)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Ateker branch: 16 principal tribes and 19 Ngoitunya & Ngolio attegir clans); documented in Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), Barton (1921), Dimmendaal (1983, 2000), and Jonathan Moodie (2016, Ch. 21, pp. 397–416, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.492).

languages.name: Embu (Kĩembu)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya southeastern slopes (Embu & Mbeere); documented in Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Hobley (1922).

languages.name: Taita (Kidawida)
languages.notes: Taita Hills Bantu (Dawida, Sagala, Kasigau); documented in Shaw (1885), Taylor (1891), Wray (1894), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Swahili (Kiswahili)
languages.notes: National & official language of Kenya (including Kiamu, Kimvita, Kitikuu/Bajuni, Kipate, Kingozi, Ki-Jezirati/Ki-Jizirat of Pemba, and Kiunguja); documented in Krapf (1850, 1882), Bishop Edward Steere (1870 'Swahili Tales, as Told by Natives of Zanzibar'), Robert Needham Cust (1883, Vol. I), Bishop Edward Steere & A. C. Madan (1894 'A Handbook of the Swahili Language, as Spoken at Zanzibar', 4th Ed.), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. I–III, pp. [v]–xx, 1–205 — audited 100% line-by-line), Taylor (1891), Bateman (1901), A. C. Madan (1903 'Swahili-English Dictionary'), Mrs. F. Burt & Rev. W. E. Taylor (1910 'Swahili Grammar and Vocabulary'), Stigand (1915), Mervyn W. H. Beech (1918 'Aids to the Study of Ki-Swahili: Four Studies Compiled and Annotated'), Werner (1918, 1919, 1933), Deo Ngonyani & Nancy Jumwa Ngowa (2016 'The productivity of the reversive extension in Standard Swahili', in Doris L. Payne, Sara Pacchiarotti & Mokaya Bosire, eds., 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 14, pp. 255–271, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.485 — audited 100% line-by-line across -u/-o/-ul/-ol & -uk/-ok, Pwani University nonce-word coinage tests [Tables 1–2] & Helsinki Corpus SALAMA acceptability judgment tests [Tables 3–4, incl. kufanyua 'to undo']), Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', in 'Diversity in African languages', Ch. 28, pp. 559–576, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.499 — audited 100% line-by-line across Vitimbi, Redykyulass, Churchill Show & Ex. 1–16), Mohamed Mwamzandi (2022 'The pragmatics of Swahili relative clauses', Language Science Press, Ch. 13, pp. 227–246), and Goldsmith & Mpiranya (2022).

languages.name: Mijikenda
languages.notes: Nine coastal Sabaki sub-groups (Giriama, Digo [Chidigo, [dig] E73], Duruma, Chonyi, Jibana, Kambe, Ribe, Rabai, Kauma); documented in Krapf (1850), Krapf & Rebmann (1887), Taylor (1891), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Steve Nicolle (2016 'Variation in the expression of information structure in eastern Bantu languages', in Doris L. Payne, Sara Pacchiarotti & Mokaya Bosire, eds., 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 20, pp. 377–395, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.491 — audited 100% line-by-line across Table 1 [864 Digo clauses from Kwale District, Kenya] & Ex. 1–30 on left/right topic dislocation, obligatory clefts for subject argument focus, and VS thetic sentences).

languages.name: Borana (Oromo)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language (Borana [including the Royal Clan Karayu of Chief Gedu in Ethiopia], Gabbra, Sakuye, Wata, and Tana River Orma — Barareta Oromo [descended from Ana Bake], Kofira Oromo [from Ana Dima/Ana Bake], and Migo Oromo [from Ana Kare]); documented in Rev. J. L. Krapf & Rev. C. W. Isenberg (1840 'An Imperfect Outline of the Elements of the Galla Language', London: CMS / L. & G. Seeley / Richard Watts, pp. [i]–xiv, [1]–16 [Bodleian Library copy] — audited 100% line-by-line; plus 1842 & 1850), Tutschek (1844–1845), Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. IX.C.II 'Galla or Orómo', pp. 122–125 — audited 100% line-by-line), Foot (1913), Werner (1915), BFBS (1921), Mikael Samson & R. G. Darroch (1944, pp. 370–394), and Griefenow-Mewis (1996).

languages.name: Rendille
languages.notes: Omo-Tana East Cushitic camel-herding pastoralists of the Kaisut and Chalbi plains (including the historical Naroshon section on the Sogota–Lomello plains); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), Fleming (1964), Heine (1976, 1978), Pillinger & Galboran (1999), and Blažek (2011).

languages.name: Teso (Ateso)
languages.notes: Eastern Nilotic (Ateker) language spoken in Busia County and eastern Uganda; documented in Hobley (1902), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Kitching (1915), Roscoe (1915), BFBS (1921), Hilders & Lawrance (1956), and Jonathan Moodie (2016 'Number marking in Lopit, an Eastern Nilotic language', in 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 397–416, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.492: Teso tripartite Singular / Plural / Greater Plural paradigm e-tunga-nan 'person' → i-tunga 'people' → i-tunga-sinei 'mankind' in Table 18, p. 412).

languages.name: Pokomo
languages.notes: Tana River (Galana Maro) Sabaki Bantu language across Malachini and Upper Pokomo; documented in Krapf (1850), Würtz (1895, 1896), Werner (1913, 1915, 1933), Johnston (1919–1922 #13 Pωkωmω), BFBS (1921), and Mikael Samson & R. G. Darroch (1944, pp. 370–394 & Full-Page Sketch Map — audited 100% line-by-line).

languages.name: Samburu
languages.notes: Northern Maa (Plains Nilotic) pastoralists (including historical Il Doigio, Lorogishu / Kwakituk on Angata e-'m-barta, Lobbeyok, and Il Leikipiak sections on the Leikipia plateau); documented in Krapf (1854), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883, Vol. I, pp. 149–152), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894, Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 367–385: traverse of the 8 Mount Kenia glacier streams, upper Guaso Nyiro, Leikipia plateau [6,000–6,850 ft.] with abandoned kraals of the Il Leikipiak routed ~20 yrs. earlier, Marmanet swamp, Ongalea mountains [172-lb elephant tusks] & Larabwal to Njemps), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Hobley (1910).

languages.name: Ilchamus (Njemps)
languages.notes: Lake Baringo Maa-speaking irrigation farmers and fishermen (Njamus / Nyarusi across Njemps Kubwa [Liabori], Njemps Ndogo [Lekepir], and Korvan, comprising 16 clans from 6 tribes); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883, Vol. I, pp. 149–152), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 367–385 [417–435] & 4 Fold-out Maps — audited 100% line-by-line across the descent via Morijo/Maza [4,650 ft.] & Mukutan gorge [3,850 ft.] to Njemps Mkubwa & Njemps Ndogo [3,220 ft., 1,500–2,000 Il Oogolala Wakwafi on the Guaso Tigerish/Perkerra & Guaso Molo], the timber-pile, brushwood & boulder dam a mile above Njemps Mkubwa with rotational earthen sluice-gate canals irrigating wimbi, mtama, melons, pumpkins, beans & tobacco, the Kerio valley grain trade with Elgeyo & Marakwet [65 loads], and the exploration of fresh-water Lake Baringo [3,190 ft., 14 × 7 mi., subterranean northern basalt drainage] & Ol Kokwa island [2½ mi., 400 ft., boiling sulphur springs] with 6–8-log ambatch oboro rafts [Herminiera elaphroxylon]), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Beech (1911).

languages.name: Pokot (Pökoot)
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Northern Kalenjin branch, historically Suk / Bawgott across 11 geographical divisions and 24 orten clans; reflexive/middle/emphatic enclitic pronounced [kɛːx] with a final velar fricative and written as a separate word in the Pökoot Bible per Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono 2024: 539–540); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), Barton (1921), Rottland (1982), and Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono (2024).

languages.name: Taveta (Kitaveta)
languages.notes: Northeast Coast Bantu (Pare-Taveta group) around Taveta and Lake Jipe; documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. II–IV, pp. 38–208 — audited 100% line-by-line across the 4-prefix Bantu rule U-/M-/Wa-/Ki- [Ta-veta/M-taveta/Wa-taveta/Ki-taveta, p. 61], the verbatim 7-turn Kiruvu greeting dialogue with Sultan Sedenga of Mkarama [p. 66], Taveta on the Lumi river [>1,500 Wataveta governed by 10 Wazee elders incl. Mkamba + agricultural Wakwafi settled ~50 yrs. earlier toward Lake Jipe], kitoweo, boys' & girls' circumcision rites, 21–22 in. pombo bead strings on Hyphæna thebaica fibre, 1,200 tailored naiberes war-mantles vs. schukas [1 doti = 2 schuka = 8 mikono, p. 141 fn. 1], Kahe speaking the identical dialect [pp. 167–169], Chaga Sultan Miriali [Mangi] of Marangu ['kilengele' & 'Tonga mbuya!', p. 113; 7 Chaga states p. 184], Mandara's Swahili taunts [pp. 198–199], Wameru Sultan Matunda's maize-ear accounting & Lake Balbal, and the June 20, 1887 ascent of Kilimanjaro to 16,240 ft. [Höhnel] & 17,387 ft. [Teleki] with Tylophora bicolor & Erigeron Telekii), Steggall (1892–1906), Hollis (1910–1911), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Daasanach (Dhaasanac)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic (Western Omo-Tana / Galaboid; autonym d’áasannæc, earlier Galab or Geleba) agropastoral and fishing community around Ileret on the northeastern shore of Lake Turkana and Southwest Ethiopia (1994 Ethiopian census: 32,029; 1980 Kenyan est.: 2,500; Tosco est.: 35,000–40,000; shares 53.3% of its 100-word core lexicon with Arbore, 50.0% with Elmolo, 38.9% with Oromo, 35.8% with Konso & Somali, and 35.6% with Rendille); documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 as Reshiat, Buma & Marle/Arbore), Gabriele da Trento (1941, 60 units), Eike Haberland (1966, 91 units), Harold C. Fleming (1965, 102 units & 1971, 146 units), M. Lionel Bender (1971, 97 units), Hans-Jürgen Sasse (1973–1984, ca. 11 studies), Mauro Tosco (2001 'The Dhaasanac Language', Kuschitische Sprachstudien Band 17, Köppe, Köln, xiv + 598 pp. + 20 photos, c. 1,400 units), Sumiyo Nishiguchi (2004 'Consonant Assimilation and Sonority : A Case Study in Daasanach', OUPEL Vol. 9, pp. 39–51, OUKA, DOI: 10.18910/70792 — audited 100% line-by-line), and Václav Blažek (2011 'Dasanech Language – State-of-the-Art', Folia Orientalia Vol. 48, Masaryk University, Brno — audited 100% line-by-line).

officialLanguages.role: Language of government, courts, higher education, and media (Article 7(2), Constitution of Kenya 2010)
National lingua franca, parliamentary co-official language, and primary language of inter-ethnic communication (Article 7(1)–(2), Constitution of Kenya 2010)

officialLanguages.language: Kenyan Sign Language (KSL), Braille & Indigenous Languages
officialLanguages.role: Protected and promoted by the State under Article 7(3) of the Constitution of Kenya 2010
